items.area: Bowling Green Drive, Golden Gate Park
items.times: Free lessons Wednesday and Saturday at noon
items.hoursFrom: sflbc.org — free lessons Wednesday and Saturday at noon
items.source: San Francisco Lawn Bowling Club; SF Rec & Park

pairings.text: Conservatory of Flowers, ten minutes east

items.why: The oldest public lawn bowling club in the country, founded in 1901 on a green in Golden Gate Park. Members teach anyone who turns up, free, on Wednesdays and Saturdays at noon, and the lesson takes about an hour. Wear flat-soled shoes, because heels ruin the green. It is gentle, oddly competitive, and nobody you know has done it.

items.title: Swim in the bay at Aquatic Park
items.area: Dolphin Club or South End Rowing Club, Jefferson Street
items.times: Public days Tuesday to Saturday, 10am to 6pm, alternating between the two clubs
items.hoursFrom: Dolphin Club and South End Rowing Club — public days Tuesday to Saturday, 10am to 6pm
items.source: South End Rowing Club; Dolphin Club; Openwaterpedia

pairings.text: Buena Vista for an Irish coffee after

items.why: Two rowing and swimming clubs from the 1870s share the beach at Aquatic Park, and on public days, Tuesday to Saturday, anyone can pay the day fee and use the sauna, showers and the cove. The water is about 55 to 62°F all year, and the regulars swim in it without wetsuits. Sign the waiver, swim along the buoys inside the breakwater, and sit in the sauna after. Check which club has the public day before you go.

items.title: Learn to surf at Linda Mar
items.priceNote: Group lessons ~$94, board and wetsuit included
items.times: Lessons most mornings — book ahead
items.hoursNote: Lessons are booked for a time, usually mornings, when the wind is lighter

pairings.text: Taco Bell Cantina on the sand, famously
Mori Point for a walk after

items.why: The gentlest surf near the city: a long, sandy cove at the south end of Pacifica, twenty minutes from San Francisco, where the waves break slowly and the bottom is sand. Nor-Cal Surf Shop, across the highway, runs lessons with the board and a thick wetsuit included. Two hours and most people stand up. Mornings are calmer; afternoons bring wind and fog.

items.title: Climbing at Movement Belmont
items.area: The old Belmont Theatre, 100 El Camino Real, Belmont
items.hoursNote: Open early to late every day — check the gym for class times
items.why: A climbing gym inside the old Belmont movie theatre, with walls going up where the screen was: about 19,000 square feet of bouldering and ropes, including real crack climbs. It is half an hour up from Palo Alto and the Peninsula's best place to start. Take the intro class, which teaches you to belay, and you can climb ropes with a friend on your own after that. Movement also has gyms in Sunnyvale, Mountain View, Santa Clara and San Francisco.

items.title: Climbing at Mission Cliffs
items.hoursNote: Open early to late every day — check the gym for class times
items.why: San Francisco's big old climbing gym, in a warehouse in the Mission: tall roped walls, a bouldering cave and a weights room. It is sociable in the evenings, when half the city's climbers come after work. Book the intro to top-rope class, and after that a day pass is all you need.

items.title: Tennis at the Golden Gate Park courts
items.area: Goldman Tennis Center, east end of Golden Gate Park
items.hoursNote: Courts by reservation — book online; SF residents can book further ahead
items.why: Seventeen courts in Golden Gate Park, rebuilt in 2021 with a clubhouse and lights for evening play. You book a court by the hour rather than queue for one, which is the whole difference from the free park courts. Clinics and lessons run for every level, if you want to start again properly.

items.title: Baylands Golf Links
items.hoursNote: Tee times from dawn — book online
items.why: Palo Alto's municipal course, rebuilt in 2018 as a links on the edge of the Baylands: no trees, marsh grass, wind off the bay and egrets on the fairways. It is fully public, and the green fees are low for the Peninsula, lower still with a Palo Alto or Bay Area ID. There is a driving range, and the Baylands trails start next door.

items.title: Ride the Hellyer Velodrome
items.priceNote: Beginner sessions and rental bikes — check the schedule
items.hoursNote: Beginner sessions on Saturday mornings
items.source: Hellyer Velodrome; Santa Clara County Parks
items.why: A banked concrete cycling track in a county park in south San Jose, built in 1962. On Saturday mornings supervisors run beginner sessions for people who have never ridden a fixed-gear track bike, and they will lend you one. The first lap on the banking, up near the rail, is frightening and then wonderful.

items.title: Kayak to McCovey Cove
items.area: South Beach Harbor, by Oracle Park
items.hoursNote: Rentals and tours from the harbour — book a slot
items.why: A kayak rental on the South Beach Harbor docks, ten minutes' paddle from McCovey Cove behind Oracle Park and up Mission Creek past the houseboats. Beginners go on the short guided trips; anyone who has paddled before can rent and go. On Giants days people float in the cove waiting for a home run to land in the water.

items.title: Kayak or paddleboard from Sausalito
items.hoursNote: Rentals daily from the marina — mornings are calmest
items.why: Paddle out from a sheltered beach in Sausalito and along Richardson Bay, past the floating houseboats and the harbour seals, with the city across the water. Rentals go by the hour and there is an intro class if you have never been in a kayak. Go in the morning: the wind comes up through the Golden Gate after lunch.

items.title: Rinconada Pool
items.hoursFrom: Palo Alto Swim — lap swim weekdays 6am to 4pm, Saturday to 5pm
items.source: Palo Alto Swim; City of Palo Alto
items.why: Palo Alto's outdoor pool in Rinconada Park: a big heated outdoor pool, open for lap swimming from six in the morning. It is the cheapest good exercise in town and the best way to start a hot day. Pay at the desk and share a lane. Check the schedule in winter, when hours shorten.

items.title: November Project
items.area: Fort Mason or Alta Plaza, early mornings
items.times: Monday and Wednesday at 6:29am; Friday hills at the Golden Gate
items.hoursNote: Monday and Wednesday at 6:29am, Fort Mason or Alta Plaza; Friday on the hills — check the group for the week
items.why: A free, loud, early workout that started in Boston and is now in dozens of cities. In San Francisco the group meets at 6:29 on Monday and Wednesday mornings, at Fort Mason or Alta Plaza, for stairs, hills and bodyweight circuits, and on the hills near the bridge on Fridays. You just show up. Somebody will hug you. It is the fastest way to meet people who run.
items.imageCredit: Original uploader was SuperJumbo at en.wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0

items.title: Disc golf in Golden Gate Park
items.area: Marx Meadow, western Golden Gate Park
items.priceNote: Free; bring or buy a disc
items.source: SF Rec & Park; PDGA course directory
items.why: Eighteen holes among the cypress and eucalyptus of western Golden Gate Park, free and open to anyone. It is golf with a frisbee: a par three is a throw between the trees to a chain basket. Any sports shop sells a starter disc for a few dollars. Weekends are busy, so let faster groups through.

items.title: The Crissy Field run
items.area: Marina Green to Fort Point and back
items.hoursFrom: Golden Gate National Recreation Area — open every day

stops.text: Start at the Marina Green, by the yacht harbour
Along the Crissy Field promenade, flat and on the water
Past the Warming Hut
Touch the fence at Fort Point, right under the bridge
Turn and run back with the city in front of you

items.why: The best run in San Francisco and one of the flattest: the old airfield along the bay from the Marina to the foot of the Golden Gate. It is four kilometres out on packed gravel, with the bridge getting bigger the whole way, and the tradition is to touch the fence at Fort Point before turning round. Go early before the wind, or at sunset when the bridge goes orange.

items.title: Lake Merced loop
items.why: A paved path all the way round the city's biggest lake, 4.5 miles with no traffic lights and almost no hills. It is where the city's runners go to do a steady long run, and one lap is a clean seven kilometres. Fog sits on it most mornings. Park on Lake Merced Boulevard and run it anticlockwise, so the lake is on your right.

items.title: The Embarcadero run
items.area: Pier 39 to Oracle Park along the water

stops.text: Start at Pier 39 — sea lions on the docks
Past the Ferry Building clock tower
Under the Bay Bridge, by Rincon Park
Turn at Oracle Park

items.why: Flat, wide and ten minutes from North Beach: the promenade along the piers from Pier 39 to the ballpark and back, about six and a half kilometres. Go before eight, while it is joggers and delivery trucks rather than crowds. On a Saturday, finish at the Ferry Building farmers' market.

items.title: Stanford Perimeter Trail
items.area: Around the Stanford campus, from Stanford Avenue or Junipero Serra
items.why: A soft-surfaced trail on the edge of the campus, along Stanford Avenue and Junipero Serra, that most Palo Alto runners use because it is flat and shaded in places and there are no cars. It is about three and a half miles, and it joins the Dish loop if you want the hills. Run it in the evening, when the foothills catch the sun.

items.title: Lands End Coastal Trail
items.area: Lands End Lookout, 680 Point Lobos Ave · 3.4 mi loop · rolling, with stairs
items.hoursFrom: Golden Gate National Recreation Area; visitor centre 9 to 5
items.source: Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy; AllTrails
items.why: The wild edge of the city: a cliff-top trail through cypress from the ruins of the Sutro Baths towards the Golden Gate, with shipwrecks below at low tide. Take the steps down to the stone labyrinth on the point and to Mile Rock Beach. The loop is about 3.4 miles with a few hundred steps. Start at the Lookout and finish with the sunset over the baths.

items.title: Mount Tam — East Peak
items.area: East Peak lot · 0.7 mi paved loop, then the Plank Trail to the lookout
items.hoursFrom: Mount Tamalpais State Park — 7am to sunset, gates locked after
items.why: The summit of the Bay without the climb: drive up Panoramic Highway to the East Peak lot and walk the Verna Dunshee loop, a flat, paved path round the top with the whole Bay, the Farallones and Mount Diablo in view. Then take the steps and the Plank Trail up to the Gardner fire lookout at the peak. Go in the afternoon, when fog often fills the valleys below you. Parking is $8, cash only.

items.title: Big Basin — the Redwood Loop
items.area: Park headquarters · 0.6 mi loop, or on to Sempervirens Falls · parking by reservation
items.hoursFrom: California State Parks — day use 8am to sunset, reservation encouraged
items.source: California State Parks; Reimagining Big Basin
items.why: California's oldest state park, which burned in the 2020 fire and is coming back. The old-growth giants around the headquarters survived. The Redwood Loop is a flat 0.6 miles past Mother of the Forest, and newly reopened trail goes on to Sempervirens Falls. Book parking online first. The long trails, Skyline-to-the-Sea included, are still closed, so do not plan on them.

items.title: Devil's Slide Trail
items.area: Between Pacifica and Montara · 1.3 mi each way · paved, bikes welcome
items.hoursFrom: San Mateo County Parks — opens at 8am, closes around sunset
items.why: A stretch of the old Highway 1 above the ocean, closed to cars when the tunnels opened in 2013 and now a paved path for walkers and bikes. It hangs on a cliff over the Pacific with seabirds nesting on the rocks below. It is flat enough for anyone and dramatic enough for everyone. Walk out to the old bunker lookout, and bring binoculars from December to April for grey whales.

items.title: Sharks and PWHL San Jose at SAP Center
items.hoursNote: Game nights, October to April — the schedule is the timetable
items.why: The Bay's hockey arena, called the Shark Tank, by the Caltrain station in downtown San Jose. The Sharks play here from October to April, and from December the PWHL's new San Jose team plays its first professional women's hockey here too. Take Caltrain to Diridon and walk across the road. The upper bowl is loud and cheap.

items.title: Earthquakes and Bay FC at PayPal Park
items.area: PayPal Park, by San Jose airport
items.hoursNote: Match days, March to November — the schedule is the timetable
items.why: An 18,000-seat football stadium with the stands right on the pitch and the largest outdoor bar in North America behind one goal. The Earthquakes play MLS here and Bay FC, the women's NWSL side, plays here too, usually Saturday or Sunday afternoons. The Caltrain stop at Santa Clara is a short walk. Stand with the supporters' groups behind the goal if you want to sing.

items.title: Stanford volleyball and basketball at Maples
items.hoursNote: Volleyball September to November, basketball November to March — the schedule is the timetable
items.why: Stanford's indoor arena, where the women's volleyball team, one of the most successful in the country, plays through the autumn, and both basketball teams play the winter. It seats about 7,000 and the student section makes it feel like more. Tickets are cheap next to anything professional. The Cal match sells out first.

items.title: Cal football at Memorial Stadium
items.hoursNote: Home games, September to November — the schedule is the timetable
items.why: A 1923 stadium set into Strawberry Canyon in the Berkeley hills, with the bay and the Golden Gate behind the west stands. Take BART to Downtown Berkeley and walk up through campus with everyone else. The game to go to is the Big Game against Stanford, which Cal hosts in even years.

items.title: Pulgas Ridge
items.area: Edgewood Road, off Interstate 280 · marked off-leash area
items.why: The Peninsula preserve where the dog can run: every trail is open to dogs, and there is a marked off-leash area (bring a leash, and keep your dog in voice control). Open grassland and oak hills, gentle walking, and the Bay in the distance.
items.dogsNote: All trails open to dogs, with a marked off-leash area; a leash must be carried and dogs kept in voice control (Midpen)
items.source: Midpen (openspace.org, dog access page); preserve position from OpenStreetMap way/38696291
items.hoursFrom: openspace.org — Midpen preserves are open from a half-hour before sunrise to a half-hour after sunset
items.hoursNote: Half an hour before sunrise until half an hour after sunset

items.title: Climbing at Movement Sunnyvale
items.why: A 28,000-square-foot climbing gym with more than 280 routes and problems, ropes up to 55 feet and a big bouldering area. It is the one on this side of the Peninsula with proper programmes for children: after-school classes for ages 6 to 8, 9 to 12 and 13 to 17, and a Kid's Climb Time for drop-off. Adults climb the same walls, so both parents can go.
items.priceNote: Day pass $35 adult, $25 child under 13, $30 student on weekdays before 5pm
items.source: movementgyms.com/sunnyvale and its youth-programs page; position from OpenStreetMap way/41935775

food.note: Food as missions rather than listings, the Paris shape. Each mission is a small assignment in a particular set of streets — candidates, what to order, how to judge, where to go afterwards. Moods map to missions in js/app.js.

items.title: An Italian Morning in North Beach
items.area: Four old Italian shops within five minutes of Washington Square
items.brief: North Beach was San Francisco's Little Italy, and a handful of the shops that fed it are still run by the same families. Start early — the focaccia sells out — and eat your way round Washington Square in the order below.
items.test: The focaccia should be soft and oily on the bottom, not bready; the cannoli shell should crack, which means it was filled after you ordered.

candidates.name: Liguria Bakery
candidates.order: A slab of plain or onion focaccia, wrapped in paper
candidates.note: Since 1911. Opens early, shuts when the trays are empty — often before noon.

candidates.name: Molinari Delicatessen
candidates.order: Take a number. A sandwich on a sweet roll for later
candidates.note: Since 1896; they cure their own salami.

candidates.name: Victoria Pastry Company
candidates.order: A cannoli, filled to order
candidates.note: Or Stella Pastry on Columbus for the sacripantina.

candidates.name: Caffe Trieste
candidates.order: A cappuccino, at a table
candidates.note: The first espresso house on the West Coast, 1956.

then.text: Eat the sandwich on the grass in Washington Square
Browse City Lights Books on Columbus

items.why: The quickest way to understand what North Beach was, and it still tastes of it. Four shops, a park and a coffee, and nothing on the list is newer than 1956.
items.hoursNote: A morning, Tuesday to Saturday — Liguria is closed Sundays and Mondays and can sell out before noon.

items.title: Chinatown, One Bite at a Time
items.area: Stockton Street and Grant Avenue, a ten-minute loop
items.priceNote: ~$25 for two — most things are a few dollars
items.brief: The oldest Chinatown in North America is at its best in the morning, when Stockton Street is doing its shopping. Eat standing up, a few dollars at a time, and finish sitting down with tea.
items.test: A good egg tart is still warm and barely set in the middle. Good dim sum to go is steamed that morning and the wrapper is thin enough to see through.

candidates.name: Golden Gate Bakery
candidates.order: Two egg tarts, warm
candidates.note: Closes without warning for weeks at a time. If there is a queue, join it.

candidates.name: Good Mong Kok Bakery
candidates.order: Har gow, siu mai and a char siu bao, to take away
candidates.note: Cash, a queue out the door, priced by the piece.

candidates.name: Red Blossom Tea Company
candidates.order: Ask them to brew an oolong tasting
candidates.note: A family tea shop on Grant since 1985.

then.text: Walk up Grant Avenue to the Dragon Gate
Sit in Portsmouth Square with the old men playing cards

items.why: Chinatown rewards the person who eats small and keeps walking. This is the cheapest good morning in San Francisco.
items.hoursNote: Best in the morning, when Stockton Street is shopping.

items.title: Settle the Burrito Argument
items.area: Three taquerias on Mission Street, within a ten-minute walk
items.brief: The Mission burrito is San Francisco's own dish, and everyone who lives here has a side. Share one burrito at each of three places — the same filling everywhere, carne asada — and decide which side you are on.
items.test: Judge the tortilla (steamed or crisped on the plancha?), the meat (charred at the edges?), and whether it holds together to the last bite. Rice is the argument.

candidates.name: La Taqueria
candidates.order: Carne asada burrito, 'dorado' style — no rice
candidates.note: The purist. No rice, crisped tortilla, a queue at lunch.

candidates.name: Taqueria El Farolito
candidates.order: Super carne asada burrito
candidates.note: The heavyweight. Open very late, and enormous.

candidates.name: Taqueria Cancún
candidates.order: Super burrito, the one with avocado
candidates.note: The comfortable one, with a salsa bar.

then.text: Walk it off to Bi-Rite Creamery, then Dolores Park
Balmy Alley murals, five minutes from La Taqueria

items.why: You will not agree with anyone afterwards, but you will know why they think what they think.
items.hoursNote: Lunch or dinner; all three open late morning.

items.title: Saturday at the Ferry Building
items.area: The farmers market around the Ferry Building, on the Embarcadero
items.priceNote: ~$50 for two, eating as you go
items.brief: On Saturday mornings the Ferry Plaza Farmers Market wraps round the Ferry Building and the best of Northern California comes to town. Go before ten, graze, buy one thing to cook, and eat lunch on the water.
items.test: Taste before you buy — every stall offers. Buy only what you could not get in a supermarket.

candidates.name: Ferry Plaza Farmers Market
candidates.step: Walk the stalls once before buying anything; stone fruit in summer, citrus in winter
candidates.note: Saturdays from 8. Also Tuesdays and Thursdays, smaller.

candidates.name: Blue Bottle Coffee, inside the Ferry Building
candidates.order: A New Orleans iced coffee

candidates.name: Hog Island Oyster Company
candidates.order: A dozen Sweetwaters at the bar
candidates.note: Queue before it opens, or eat at the counter outside.

then.text: Walk the Embarcadero north towards Pier 39 and the sea lions
Take the F-line streetcar back along the water

items.why: San Francisco is a food city because of what grows within a hundred miles of it. This is where you see that.
items.hoursNote: Saturday, 8 until 2 — go before ten.

items.title: The Palo Alto Croissant Test
items.area: Three bakeries between Lytton Avenue and Town & Country
items.brief: Palo Alto has quietly got very good at laminated dough. Buy one plain croissant at each — plain, or the test means nothing — and eat them within the hour.
items.test: Does it shatter when torn, is the inside honeycombed rather than bready, and does it taste of butter after you swallow?

candidates.name: Mademoiselle Colette
candidates.order: Plain croissant, then the almond one
candidates.note: The French one, on Lytton.

candidates.name: Manresa Bread
candidates.order: Plain croissant, and a loaf for later
candidates.note: From the team behind the Michelin-starred Manresa.

candidates.name: La Baguette
candidates.order: Plain croissant
candidates.note: The one in the Stanford Shopping Center.

then.text: Reset with a coffee at Coupa Café on Ramona
Eat the winner in the Rodin Sculpture Garden at Stanford

items.why: The same hour you would spend in Paris, and you will come out knowing which bakery is yours.
items.hoursNote: A morning — bakeries run low on croissants by midday.

items.title: Three Scoops on University
items.area: University Avenue and the Stanford Shopping Center, an evening walk
items.brief: Palo Alto takes its ice cream seriously and the good ones are a short walk apart. One small scoop at each, the same flavour family everywhere — something with caramel or pistachio — and a walk in between.
items.test: Judge on texture first (dense and elastic, or light and icy?), then whether the flavour tastes of the thing rather than of sugar.

candidates.name: Scoop Microcreamery
candidates.order: One small scoop, their seasonal flavour

candidates.name: Bacio di Latte
candidates.order: Pistachio gelato
candidates.note: At the Stanford Shopping Center, a pleasant walk along El Camino.

candidates.name: The Penny Ice Creamery
candidates.order: Anything with the torched marshmallow
candidates.note: In Town & Country, across El Camino.

then.text: Walk back down University after dark, when the trees are lit

items.why: An evening walk with a reason to it — and a genuinely different ice cream at each stop.
items.hoursNote: An evening, after dinner.

items.title: Noodles on Castro Street
items.area: Castro Street, Mountain View — all within two blocks
items.brief: Castro Street is one of the best noodle streets on the Peninsula. Share a bowl at each place across an evening — handmade Japanese udon, then northern Chinese hand-cut noodles and dumplings.
items.test: The noodle is the whole test: bounce and bite, whether it holds the sauce, and whether it was made in the building.

candidates.name: Udon Mugizo
candidates.order: Mentaiko cream udon, or kake udon with tempura
candidates.note: Handmade udon. Queue at lunch.

candidates.name: Seasons Noodle & Dumpling Garden
candidates.order: Hand-cut noodles and a plate of dumplings

then.text: Finish at Red Rock Coffee at the top of Castro
Caltrain is at the bottom of the street

items.why: The most convincing evidence that the best food in Silicon Valley is on its main streets, not its campuses.
items.hoursNote: An evening; Udon Mugizo has the longest queue at lunch.

items.title: Sunday Market, Castro Street Pastry
items.area: The Caltrain station lot and the top of Castro Street
items.brief: On Sunday mornings the Mountain View farmers market fills the Caltrain lot. Walk it first, buy fruit and something hot, then take it up Castro Street for coffee and pastry.
items.test: At the market: buy what is at the peak of its season and nothing else. At Maison Alyzée: the plain croissant decides it.

candidates.name: Mountain View Farmer's Market
candidates.step: One lap before you buy. Hot food at the far end.
candidates.note: Sundays, mornings only.

candidates.name: Maison Alyzée
candidates.order: Croissant and a kouign-amann

candidates.name: Dana Street Roasting Company
candidates.order: A house espresso, and a bag of beans for the week

then.text: Pioneer Park, behind the library, for a picnic

items.why: A proper Sunday morning without leaving the South Bay.
items.hoursNote: Sunday morning — the market packs up around 1.

items.title: Dumplings, Then Dessert, at Santana Row
items.area: Valley Fair and Santana Row, facing each other across Stevens Creek
items.brief: Put your name down at Din Tai Fung in Valley Fair, wander Santana Row across the road while you wait, eat dumplings, then walk the Row for dessert — one thing each, shared.
items.test: Xiao long bao: lift it by the knot without tearing it, and the soup should be hot and clear. Dessert: pick the one you cannot get anywhere else in the South Bay.

candidates.name: Din Tai Fung
candidates.order: Pork xiao long bao, spicy wontons, the green beans
candidates.note: Join the waitlist online before you arrive.

candidates.name: Smitten Ice Cream
candidates.order: Salted caramel, churned to order

candidates.name: Lady M
candidates.order: A slice of green tea mille crêpes
candidates.note: Back in Valley Fair, near Din Tai Fung.

candidates.name: SomiSomi
candidates.order: Ube soft serve in a taiyaki cone
candidates.note: The alternative to Lady M.

then.text: Sit by the fire pits in the middle of the Row

items.why: A night out that is easy to plan and hard to get wrong.
items.hoursNote: An evening; the Din Tai Fung queue is shortest before 6.

items.title: An Evening on Broadway
items.area: Three stops along Broadway, downtown Redwood City, within a ten-minute walk
items.brief: Downtown Redwood City does a good evening on one street. Start with a beer and a pretzel in a German beer garden, walk down Broadway to wood-fired pizza, and finish with a scoop of odd ice cream a few doors on.
items.test: The pizza decides it: a blistered, chewy crust that still holds its shape in the middle. The ice cream should taste of what the name says, however strange that is.

candidates.name: Gourmet Haus Staudt
candidates.order: A German beer on tap and a soft pretzel with mustard
candidates.note: The beer garden is out the back; the German grocery at the front is worth a look.

candidates.name: Vesta
candidates.order: One pizza from the wood oven and a small plate to share
candidates.note: Busy at dinner. Closed Sundays.

candidates.name: Humphry Slocombe
candidates.order: Secret Breakfast — bourbon and cornflakes

then.text: Sit on the steps of Courthouse Square with the ice cream
Or a late cocktail at LV Mar, next door to Vesta

items.why: A proper night out without driving anywhere. Three good places, one street, and each stop sets up the next.
items.hoursNote: Tuesday to Saturday evening. Vesta is closed Sundays, and the beer garden closes at 8 on Mondays.

items.title: A Taiwanese Sunday in Cupertino
items.area: Stevens Creek Boulevard, from Liang’s Village to De Anza College
items.brief: Cupertino is one of the best places outside Taiwan to eat like you are in Taipei. Start with a Taiwanese breakfast, walk the Sunday farmers market at De Anza College, then finish with a properly brewed tea.
items.test: Breakfast: the fried cruller should be crisp, and the soy milk made in-house. Tea: order the oolong without much sugar, so you can taste whether it was brewed to order.

candidates.name: Liang’s Village
candidates.order: Taiwanese breakfast: warm soy milk, a fried cruller, a scallion pancake
candidates.note: Breakfast is Friday to Sunday from 8. Beef noodle soup is on from 11.

candidates.name: De Anza College Farmers’ Market
candidates.step: One lap first, then Asian greens and whatever fruit is in season
candidates.note: Sundays 9 to 1.

candidates.name: Chicha San Chen
candidates.order: An oolong or Dong Ding milk tea, low sugar
candidates.note: Opens at 11:30. Expect a queue.

then.text: Take a dozen from Donut Wheel home — it never closes
Or a proper espresso at Voyager Craft Coffee

items.why: A morning that shows what Cupertino is really good at, and costs very little.
items.hoursNote: Sunday morning only: breakfast from 8, the market 9 to 1, tea from 11:30.

itineraries.note: Ready-made routes. Each is a sequence, not a list — the order matters. Researched from the records they name; walk one and rewrite it in your own words.

items.title: An afternoon at Stanford
items.why: Everything on it is free, and it is the best-looking square mile on the Peninsula. Rodin first, then the Cantor while you are standing next to it, then the Cactus Garden, tucked into the arboretum and easy to miss.

stops.text: The Rodin Sculpture Garden — The Gates of Hell, in the open air
The Cantor Arts Center next door, free
Across the Oval to the Main Quad and Memorial Church
The Arizona Cactus Garden, hidden in the arboretum

items.title: Saturday morning downtown
items.why: The farmers' market is only on Saturday and only in the morning, so it goes first. After that it is a slow loop through the downtown that is on the site.

stops.text: The farmers' market on Gilman Street — fruit, bread, cheese, flowers
Coffee upstairs at Goodthing on Ramona
An almond croissant at Mademoiselle Colette on Lytton
Down to Addison Avenue for the HP Garage, from the sidewalk

items.title: North Beach and the Filbert Steps
items.why: Up Telegraph Hill the front way and down it the back way, through gardens you can't see from the street. The stairs are steep, so do it in this direction.

stops.text: City Lights on Columbus — the Beats, upstairs in the poetry room
A box of dim sum from Good Mong Kok on Stockton
Washington Square, under the church
Up Filbert Street to Coit Tower
Down the Filbert Steps through the cottage gardens to the bay

items.title: Lands End to the Sutro Baths
items.why: The wildest walk inside the city limits: a cliff trail through cypress with the Golden Gate opening up ahead, ending at the ruins of a Victorian bathhouse. Do it late afternoon and stay for the sunset.

stops.text: Start at the Sutro Baths ruins, below the Lands End lookout
East along the Lands End Trail, through the cypress
The Golden Gate from the cliff at Eagle’s Point
Back to the baths for sunset over the Pacific

daytrips.note: Driving times are off-peak and only a guide: the Bay Bridge, 101 and Highway 17 can double them. Each trip carries a time from both bases — North Beach and Palo Alto — and the site shows the one nearer to wherever you are. Each says what to do there, in order, and when it is worth going; the ones marked overnight are weekends, not days. Anything with a booking says so. Researched, not yet done — rate them as you go.

items.title: Filoli
items.transit: Drive up Cañada Road, 20 min
items.why: A Georgian Revival house and sixteen acres of formal gardens on 654 acres of the Santa Cruz foothills: a walled garden, an orchard and trails into the nature reserve behind it. It is the nearest real outing from Palo Alto and it changes by season. Autumn Days brings giant pumpkins and cider, and the house is dressed for the holidays from November. Book tickets online.

items.title: Half Moon Bay & the coast
items.transit: Highway 92 over the hill, about 40 min
items.why: The nearest ocean: over the hill on 92 and you are in fog and cypress. Walk the coastal trail and go out to Pillar Point, where the Mavericks surf break sits offshore. Buy fish off the boats in the harbour. In mid-October the town's Art & Pumpkin Festival takes over Main Street and 92 jams all day, so go another weekend.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The Coastal Trail along the bluffs
Pillar Point, looking out at the Mavericks break
Fish straight off the boats at Pillar Point Harbor
Half Moon Bay Brewing on the harbour for the view

items.season: Autumn is the clearest. Avoid the Art & Pumpkin Festival weekend in mid-October unless that is the plan.
items.dogsNote: On a lead on the Coastside Trail and in the picnic areas; not on the state beaches

items.title: Santa Cruz
items.priceNote: Free to walk; rides and parks extra
items.transit: Highway 17 over the mountains, about 50 min, much longer on summer weekends
items.why: Three kinds of day in one town. There is the Boardwalk, with the 1924 Giant Dipper, one of the oldest wooden roller coasters still running. There is West Cliff Drive, a walk along the cliffs to the surfers at Steamer Lane. And ten minutes inland, the old-growth redwoods of Henry Cowell. Go early: 17 is slow in both directions on a sunny weekend.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The Boardwalk and the 1924 Giant Dipper
West Cliff Drive to Steamer Lane to watch the surfers
Natural Bridges at the end of West Cliff, for tide pools
Henry Cowell redwoods on the way home, ten minutes inland

items.season: All year. Monarch butterflies winter at Natural Bridges from October to February.
items.dogsNote: On a lead along West Cliff Drive and on It’s Beach; not in the Boardwalk

items.title: Muir Woods
items.transit: Through San Francisco and over the Golden Gate, about 75 min
items.why: Old-growth coast redwoods in a canyon under Mount Tamalpais, made a national monument in 1908. The flat boardwalk loop is short. Take the Dipsea or Ben Johnson trail up the side of the canyon to get away from the crowd. You cannot just turn up: parking and the shuttle both need a reservation, every day, at gomuirwoods.com.
items.hoursFrom: nps.gov — 8am to around sunset, every day
items.hoursNote: 8am to sunset

stops.text: Reserve parking or the shuttle at gomuirwoods.com first
The boardwalk loop along Redwood Creek
Up the Ben Johnson trail to get away from the crowd
The Pelican Inn at Muir Beach, ten minutes down the road

items.season: All year. Winter brings spawning salmon to Redwood Creek; weekday mornings are quietest.
items.dogsNote: No pets in Muir Woods or on the trails around it

items.title: Napa Valley
items.transit: About 1h45 via the Bay Bridge or the San Mateo Bridge and I-880
items.why: The valley is thirty miles of vineyards between two ridges, and a good day is two or three wineries, not six. Most tastings are by appointment now, so book them before you drive. Have lunch at the Oxbow Public Market in the town of Napa, and take the Silverado Trail rather than Highway 29 when 29 is jammed. Somebody has to not drink: plan who drives, or stay the night.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours; most wineries want a tasting booked ahead

stops.text: Leave by nine. From the city, over the Golden Gate and through Sonoma, about 75 min
A first tasting at ten or eleven, booked — Yountville or Oakville
Lunch at Oxbow Public Market in Napa, or Oakville Grocery on 29
One more tasting, reached by the Silverado Trail when 29 is jammed
Or finish at the top of the valley in Calistoga, with a mud bath at the hot springs

items.season: Harvest, late August to October, is the best and busiest. January to March is mustard season: yellow between the vines, quiet and cheaper.

items.title: Monterey & Point Lobos
items.transit: US-101 south and Highway 156, about 1h40
items.why: The Monterey Bay Aquarium, on Cannery Row, is the reason to come: the kelp forest tank is three storeys tall. Then go south to Point Lobos, the rockiest, greenest few miles of the coast, where sea otters float in the coves. Point Lobos is moving to reservations for every visitor this year, so check before you go. Carmel is five minutes on and has a card of its own.
items.hoursNote: A day of two places — the aquarium sells timed tickets, and Point Lobos keeps state-park daylight hours

stops.text: Monterey Bay Aquarium when it opens — the kelp forest feeding and the otters first
Lunch on Cannery Row or Fisherman's Wharf
Point Lobos: the Cypress Grove and Sea Lion Point trails — check reservations
Sunset on Carmel Beach, five minutes on

items.season: All year. Autumn is the clearest and warmest on the coast; summer is often foggy.

items.title: Point Reyes
items.transit: Over the Golden Gate and out through Marin, about 2 hours
items.why: A peninsula of cliffs, beaches and cattle ranches. Walk down to the lighthouse, 300-odd steps below the headland. From December to March, elephant seals haul out at Chimney Rock. Tomales Bay oysters, eaten at the water's edge, are the lunch. It is windy and cold out there even when Palo Alto is hot, so bring a layer.
items.hoursFrom: nps.gov — the seashore is open 6am to midnight

stops.text: Hog Island or the Marshall Store on Tomales Bay for oysters at the water
Point Reyes Station, the one-street town, for bread and cheese for the day
Out to the lighthouse and down the 300-odd steps — closed in high wind
Chimney Rock for elephant seals, December to March
Or north to Tomales Point for the tule elk

items.season: All year. Winter has the seals and grey whales; spring the wildflowers on Chimney Rock.

items.title: Big Sur
items.priceNote: Mostly free; state parks ~$10 a car
items.transit: Through Carmel and down Highway 1, about 2h30 to Bixby Bridge
items.why: The drive is the point: Highway 1 on cliffs over the Pacific. Bixby Bridge (1932) is the famous view. At Julia Pfeiffer Burns, McWay Falls drops onto a beach you are not allowed to reach, which somehow makes it better. It is a long day there and back, and better as a night away. The road closes for landslides most winters, so check Caltrans before you set off.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours; check Highway 1 before you set off

stops.text: Bixby Bridge, the famous view, from the turnout on the north side
Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park for a redwood walk and lunch
McWay Falls at Julia Pfeiffer Burns, a short walk from the car park
Sunset from Nepenthe's terrace, then a night in the woods

items.season: Spring and autumn. Winter landslides close Highway 1 most years — check Caltrans before you leave.

items.title: Lake Tahoe
items.priceNote: A weekend: lodging is the cost
items.transit: About 4 hours via I-80 or US-50 — a weekend, not a day
items.why: A clear alpine lake in the Sierra, and a weekend rather than a day. In summer, Emerald Bay and the beaches. In winter, the ski resorts. Friday-evening traffic out of the Bay is the real obstacle, so leave early or on Saturday morning. In winter, chain controls on 80 and 50 are routine: carry chains or have four-wheel drive.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Emerald Bay from the overlook on Highway 89, then down to Vikingsholm
The Rubicon Trail along the shore to D.L. Bliss
Sand Harbor on the Nevada side for the clearest water
In winter: a day at Palisades, Northstar or Heavenly instead

items.season: Summer for the lake, December to April for skiing. Carry chains in winter.

items.title: Yosemite Valley
items.transit: About 4 hours via I-580 and Highway 120 — a weekend, not a day
items.why: Granite walls three thousand feet high: El Capitan, Half Dome, and waterfalls that run hardest in late spring. It needs a weekend. Book somewhere to sleep well ahead, because the valley fills up. The park has used entry reservations at peak times in recent years, so check nps.gov for your dates before you go.
items.hoursFrom: nps.gov — open all day, every day; no entry reservation in 2026

stops.text: Lower Yosemite Fall, a flat mile from the valley floor
The Mist Trail to Vernal Fall — steep, wet, and the best half-day in the park
El Capitan Meadow, looking for climbers on the wall
Tunnel View at sunset
Glacier Point next morning, when the road is open

items.season: Late spring for the waterfalls, autumn for fewer people. Tioga and Glacier Point roads close in winter; check reservations for peak dates.

items.title: Capitola
items.priceNote: Free; parking metered in the village
items.transit: Highway 17 to Santa Cruz, then ten minutes east — about 50 min from Palo Alto
items.why: The nearest thing to the Italian Riviera in California. The Venetian Court is two rows of candy-coloured stucco houses right on the sand, built in 1924 and listed on the National Register. The beach sits in a sheltered cove, so the water is gentler than anywhere else on this coast. It was California's first seaside resort, in 1874. Walk the wharf, eat in the village, and swim if you're brave.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours
items.dogsNote: No dogs on Capitola beach, by city ordinance

items.title: Carmel-by-the-Sea
items.transit: US-101 and Highway 1 through Monterey, about 1h45
items.why: A village that looks like an English storybook. In the 1920s Hugh Comstock built fairytale cottages here, with swooping roofs and stone chimneys, and the houses still go by names rather than street numbers. Walk the lanes to find Hansel and Gretel, then down to Carmel Beach: white sand under wind-bent cypress, and dogs off the lead. Pair it with Point Lobos, five minutes south.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

items.title: Sausalito by ferry
items.transit: The ferry from the Ferry Building, about 30 min across the bay
items.why: Go by boat, not by car: the ferry from the Ferry Building crosses the bay past Alcatraz with the Golden Gate on your left. Sausalito is a hillside town over the water. Walk the waterfront, then out to the floating houseboat community on Richardson Bay. Take the ferry back at sunset.
items.hoursNote: The ferry runs to a timetable — goldengate.org/ferry has it

items.title: Año Nuevo elephant seals
items.priceNote: Guided walk + parking, booked ahead in winter
items.transit: Down Highway 1 past Pescadero, about 55 min from Palo Alto
items.why: The largest mainland breeding colony of elephant seals in the world, on a windswept point down the coast. In winter the bulls fight on the beach and the pups are born. From December 15 to March 31 you can only go on a docent-led walk of three to four miles, and those book out, so reserve on ReserveCalifornia the day they open. From April to November you can walk out on your own.
items.hoursNote: The seals are seen on guided walks only, 15 December to 31 March, booked on ReserveCalifornia up to 56 days ahead
items.dogsNote: No pets anywhere in the park, and not left in the car

items.title: Fitzgerald tide pools
items.transit: Highway 1 to Moss Beach, 15 min north of Half Moon Bay
items.why: Some of the richest tide pooling on the California coast, in Moss Beach. Time it to a low tide of one foot or less, best an hour or two before the lowest point. Then the reef is uncovered and full of giant green anemones, purple sea stars, urchins and hermit crabs, with harbour seals on the rocks. Check a tide table before you go, wear shoes with grip, and bring a jacket. Volunteer naturalists are there at weekends.
items.hoursNote: Opens at 8am every day and closes between 5pm and 8pm with the season; go at low tide
items.dogsNote: No dogs at the tide pools; only on the Coastal Trail above them, on a lead

items.title: Pescadero and Pigeon Point
items.transit: Highway 84 over the hills through La Honda, about 55 min
items.why: A farm town of a few hundred people a mile in from the sea, and the easiest family day on this coast. Buy a warm loaf of artichoke-garlic bread at Arcangeli Grocery, baking here since 1929, and say hello to the goats over the fence at Harley Farms. Then go down to the tide pools at Bean Hollow and on to Pigeon Point, one of the tallest lighthouses on the West Coast. Its tower is closed, but the grounds and the view along the cliffs are open every day.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door. Harley Farms welcomes visitors 11am to 4pm daily; the lighthouse grounds are open 8am to sunset

stops.text: Artichoke-garlic bread at Arcangeli Grocery on Stage Road
The goats over the fence at Harley Farms, and the cheese shop
Tide pools at Bean Hollow State Beach, down the coast
Pigeon Point Light Station and the clifftop path

items.season: Any clear day. Go at low tide for Bean Hollow, and from December to April look out for grey whales passing Pigeon Point.
items.dogsNote: On a lead at Bean Hollow and by the pond at Harley Farms; not on Pescadero State Beach, in the marsh, at the goats or on the lighthouse grounds

items.title: Solvang and the Santa Ynez Valley
items.transit: US-101 south the whole way, about 4 hours from Palo Alto — a weekend
items.why: A Danish village in the Santa Ynez Valley, founded in 1911 by Danish-Americans who wanted a folk school in the sun: half-timbered houses, windmills, and bakeries selling kringle. It sounds like a theme park and is actually a real town. The valley around it is wine country, the one in the film Sideways, and the reason to stay the night. Pair it with Santa Barbara, forty minutes over the pass.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Æbleskiver from the outdoor window at Solvang Restaurant on Alisal Road
Kringle and a cardamom bun at one of the Copenhagen Drive bakeries
Elverhøj Museum, a Danish farmhouse built by hand — Thursday to Monday, 11 to 5, $5
Mission Santa Inés, founded 1804, at the edge of town
Ten minutes up the road: the tasting rooms of Los Olivos, a one-street town
Sunset in the vineyards on Foxen Canyon Road

items.season: All year. Danish Days, the third weekend of September, is the big one; December brings the Julefest lights. Spring is green and summer is hot inland.

items.title: Paso Robles
items.transit: US-101 south through Salinas, about 2h50 from Palo Alto — a weekend
items.why: Napa before it was Napa: two hundred wineries in the oak hills halfway to Los Angeles, most of them run by the people pouring, and tastings that cost half as much. Go for the reds, the Rhône grapes and the zinfandel. The town square is a proper small-town park ringed with places to eat. Stay a night, because the best thing here happens after dark.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Tin City: a dozen small wineries, a brewery and a cidery in corrugated-iron warehouses — walk between them
Lunch on the downtown square
An afternoon tasting out on Highway 46 West, booked
Sensorio's Field of Light after dark: 58,800 solar-lit glass spheres on a hillside — book the time slot
Next morning, 40 minutes over the hill to the coast at Cambria

items.season: Harvest in September and October is the best time. Summer days are hot, well over 90°F. Winter is quiet and cheaper.
items.imageSubject: Vineyards in the Paso Robles AVA

items.title: Hearst Castle and Cambria
items.priceNote: Grand Rooms tour ~$35; the seals are free
items.transit: US-101 to Paso Robles, then Highway 46 to the coast, about 3h30 — a weekend
items.why: William Randolph Hearst's hilltop palace above the sea, built from 1919 to 1947 and filled with ceilings and choir stalls bought from Spanish monasteries. You can only see it on a tour, and the Grand Rooms tour takes seventy minutes, up about 140 steps. Book it ahead. The coast road below has an elephant seal beach and the pine-wooded village of Cambria for the night.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The Grand Rooms tour: the Assembly Room, the Refectory, the Neptune Pool from above — book up to 60 days ahead
Piedras Blancas, ten minutes north: thousands of elephant seals on the beach below the boardwalk, free
Harmony, pop. 18, for a coffee on the way back
Moonstone Beach boardwalk in Cambria at sunset
Drive home up Highway 1 through Big Sur, if the road is open

items.season: All year. The elephant seal pups are born in January and February, when the beach is fullest. The castle is decorated for the holidays in December.

items.title: Sonoma and Healdsburg
items.transit: Over the Golden Gate and up 101, about an hour to Sonoma from the city
items.why: The easier wine country. The town of Sonoma is built round a leafy plaza where California briefly declared itself a republic in 1846, and the last of the missions stands on one corner. Healdsburg, an hour north, is the other plaza, with the best food in the county and the Russian River and Dry Creek valleys at the end of every street. Do one or the other, not both, and book tastings.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Sonoma Plaza and Mission San Francisco Solano, the last of the 21 missions, 1823
Picnic from the cheese shops on the plaza
One tasting in the Sonoma Valley, booked
Or skip on to Healdsburg: lunch off the plaza, then Dry Creek Valley zinfandel
A swim or a paddle in the Russian River in summer

items.season: Harvest, August to October, is the prettiest and busiest. Spring has the mustard and the wildflowers.

items.title: Mendocino and Fort Bragg
items.priceNote: The headlands are free; the Skunk Train is extra
items.transit: US-101 to Cloverdale, then Highway 128 through Anderson Valley, about 3h15 from the city — a weekend
items.why: A New England fishing village on a headland over the Pacific, with water towers, picket fences and the whole town inside a state park. The drive up is part of it: Highway 128 through the vineyards of Anderson Valley and a redwood tunnel to the sea. Stay two nights. Fort Bragg, ten miles north, has the railway and the glass beach.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Anderson Valley on the way up: apple stands and Alsatian-style wine in Philo
Walk the cliffs of Mendocino Headlands State Park, all around the town
Point Cabrillo Light Station, a mile of path to a lighthouse from 1909
The Skunk Train from Fort Bragg into the redwoods, or the railbikes along Pudding Creek — book ahead
Glass Beach in Fort Bragg: sea-worn glass from an old dump. Look, don't take — it is a state park

items.season: All year. Whales pass from December to April. Summer is foggy on the coast and hot 20 minutes inland.

items.title: Santa Barbara
items.priceNote: Mostly free; the Funk Zone tasting rooms extra
items.transit: US-101 south, about 4h40 from Palo Alto — a weekend, or pair with Solvang
items.why: A Spanish-colonial town between the mountains and the sea, rebuilt in white stucco and red tile after the 1925 earthquake. It is a different California from the Bay: warmer, slower, and in bloom. Climb the courthouse tower, walk the wharf, and spend the evening in the Funk Zone, where the wineries have tasting rooms in old warehouses a block from the beach.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: The County Courthouse: free, and the clock tower has the view over the whole town
Old Mission Santa Barbara, "Queen of the Missions", on the hill
Stearns Wharf and the beach path along Cabrillo Boulevard
The Funk Zone at dusk: the Urban Wine Trail, a dozen tasting rooms on foot
Next morning, Solvang for breakfast on the way home

items.season: All year; it is warmer than the Bay in every month. June is cool and grey here too.

items.title: Pinnacles National Park
items.transit: US-101 to Gilroy, then Highway 25 to the east entrance, about 1h45
items.why: The remains of an ancient volcano, torn in half by the San Andreas Fault: rock spires, talus caves you walk through with a torch, and California condors riding the thermals overhead. It is the nearest national park and the least visited. It is too hot in summer; go between October and May. Use the east entrance, because the two sides do not connect by road.
items.hoursNote: Open all day — the east entrance is the one for the caves and the High Peaks

stops.text: Start early at the east entrance; the Bear Gulch lot fills by ten at weekends
Bear Gulch Cave: a scramble through boulders in the dark — bring a torch, and check it is open (it closes for bats)
Bear Gulch Reservoir, above the cave
The High Peaks trail: steps cut into the rock and handrails, and the best chance of condors
Home via Hollister, or the fruit stands on 25 in summer

items.season: October to May. Spring brings wildflowers; summer is regularly over 100°F. Check the cave status on nps.gov before you go.
items.dogsNote: Not on any trail; only on roads, picnic areas and the campground

items.title: Angel Island
items.transit: Golden Gate Ferry from the Ferry Building, about 30 min — or the short ferry from Tiburon
items.why: The biggest island in the bay, a state park you can only reach by boat. A five-mile road loops round it with a view of the Golden Gate, the city, Alcatraz and Mount Tam in turn. On the far side is the Immigration Station, where from 1910 to 1940 Chinese immigrants were held, sometimes for months, and carved poems into the barracks walls. They are still there. Check the ferry times first: there are only a few sailings a day.
items.hoursNote: A place to spend the day, not a door — what is in it keeps its own hours

stops.text: Ferry to Ayala Cove — from the Ferry Building, or from Tiburon
Walk or cycle the Perimeter Road, 5 miles, with the whole bay in turn
The Immigration Station and its poems, on the north-east side
Or climb Mount Livermore, 788 feet, for the view from the middle of the bay
Picnic back at Ayala Cove before the last boat

items.season: All year, weekends especially. The Blue & Gold boat from Pier 41 is suspended in 2026, so use the Ferry Building or Tiburon.
items.dogsNote: No dogs on the island; service animals only

Kinjo was a Japanese restaurant in Russian Hill, San Francisco, in the U.S. state of California.
Old Mandarin Islamic Restaurant is a Chinese restaurant in San Francisco's Sunset District that specializes in Uyghur cuisine.
Cortez was a restaurant in San Francisco. It received a Michelin star before closing in 2008.
Ssal is a Korean restaurant in San Francisco, California. The restaurant has received a Michelin star.
Dio Deka is a restaurant in Los Gatos, California. The restaurant serves Greek/Hellenic/Mediterranean cuisine and has received a Michelin star.
Rich Table is a restaurant in Hayes Valley, San Francisco, in the U.S. state of California. The restaurant serves American / Californian / New American cuisine.
Bar Crenn, specifically Le Comptoir at Bar Crenn, is a Michelin-starred bar and restaurant in San Francisco, California.
Plumed Horse is a restaurant in Saratoga, California, United States. The restaurant serves New American cuisine and has received a Michelin star.
La Folie was a French restaurant in Russian Hill, San Francisco, in the U.S. state of California. The fine dining establishment had received a Michelin star, before closing in 2020.
All Spice is a restaurant in San Mateo, California, United States. The restaurant has received a Michelin star.
Prik Hom is a Thai restaurant in San Francisco, California. Established in February 2023, the business was included in The New York Times's 2023 list of the 50 best restaurants in the United States.

Noodle in a Haystack is a Japanese restaurant in San Francisco, California. Established in April 2022, the business was included in The New York Times's 2023 list of the 50 best restaurants in the United States.

Pellier Park, is a city park covering 0.5 acres (0.20 ha) in San Jose, California, United States, located in close proximity to San Pedro Square. Park in San Jose, California, United States. Established 2023.

Saratoga Village Library, formerly known as the Saratoga Library, is a historic building in Saratoga, California designed by architect Eldridge T. Spencer in 1927. The building is historically significant due to its long association with the development of civic life of Saratoga throughout the 20th  A listed building.
The Roma Bakery is a bakery located in San Jose, California built by Vittorio Pera in 1911. The building's architectural style is a blend of Colonial Revival and Queen Anne. A listed building.
Piglet & Co is a Taiwanese restaurant in San Francisco, California. It was named one of twelve best new restaurants in the U.S. by Eater in 2023.

Pillar Point Bluff is a 220-acre park (89 ha) in San Mateo County, California. It is part of the Fitzgerald Marine Reserve, owned by the U.S. state of California, and managed by San Mateo County as a county park and nature preserve.
Ame was a restaurant in San Francisco, California. The restaurant had received a Michelin star, before closing in 2016.
One Market was a restaurant in San Francisco, California, United States. It closed permanently on June 11, 2025.
Omakase is a Japanese restaurant in the South of Market neighborhood in San Francisco, California. The 14-seat restaurant, owned by Kash Feng and chef Jackson Yu, has earned a Michelin star.

Mourad was a Moroccan restaurant in San Francisco, California, United States. It was founded by chef Mourad Lahlou in 2015, and is located in the former Pacific Telephone Building at 140 New Montgomery Street in the SoMA neighborhood.
Koi Palace is a Chinese restaurant in Daly City, California. It was a semifinalist in the Outstanding Restaurant category of the James Beard Foundation Awards.
The Alameda Naval Air Museum is an aviation museum located in Alameda, California and focused on the history of Naval Air Station Alameda.

La Mejor Bakery is a Mexican bakery located in the Mission District of San Francisco, California, in the United States. The bakery was recognized as a San Francisco legacy business in 2024 after 30 years of continuous operation at its sole location at 3329 24th Street.

China Basin Park is a 5-acre (2.0 ha) park in San Francisco, California, located at the mouth of Mission Creek in the Mission Bay neighborhood and across from the Oracle Park baseball stadium. The park features a hilly lawn, dog run, artificial beach, amphitheater seating, and a statue of Willie McC

The Tool Box was a leather bar for gay men in San Francisco that operated from 1962 to 1971 on the east corner of 4th Street and Harrison Street. It was the first leather bar in the South of Market, and a meeting spot where influential personalities of the early San Francisco leather scene gathered.
Aphotic was a seafood restaurant on Folsom Street in the SoMa neighborhood of San Francisco, California, with one Michelin star. It opened in March 2023 and closed in December 2024.
Park in San Francisco, California, United States.

Sunset Dunes is a 2 mi (3.2 km) long public urban park next to Ocean Beach on the West Side of San Francisco, California. The park is located on a former location of the Great Highway between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard.

Chef Chu's is a Chinese-American restaurant in Los Altos, California, owned by chef Lawrence Chu. PLS on Post is a restaurant in San Francisco, California, United States. Sage Hospitality Group opened the restaurant in late August 2022, serving American cuisine such as hamburgers, milkshakes, and French fries.
The Grand Theater is a historic theater in the Mission District of San Francisco, California. The venue became San Francisco Historic Landmark #315 in March 2024.
Hilda and Jesse is a Michelin-starred, queer-owned restaurant in the North Beach neighborhood of San Francisco, California, United States. Previously a pop-up, the restaurant opened in November 2021.
Smuggler's Cove is a tiki bar in the Hayes Valley neighborhood of San Francisco, California, United States. It was founded in 2009 by Martin Cate, who now co-owns the bar with his wife Rebecca.
Edinburgh Castle Pub was a dive bar in San Francisco, California, United States. It closed permanently in 2025.

Chez TJ was a French restaurant in Mountain View, California, United States. Opened in 1982 and closed in 2026, it was located in a historic house and until 2025 had a Michelin star; from 2007 to 2009, it had two stars.
The Museum of San Francisco is a non-profit history museum focused on the history of the city of San Francisco located in the San Francisco Financial District.
The Tenderloin Museum is a cultural center dedicated to the history of the Tenderloin neighborhood in San Francisco.

Belli Building is a historic multi-use building, built in c. 1851 in the Jackson Square neighborhood at 722–728 Montgomery Street in San Francisco, California. After the 1989 earthquake, the Belli Building and the adjacent Genella Building were damaged and left vacant for many years, and subsequentl
Sushi Shin is a Japanese restaurant in Redwood City, California, United States. It has received a Michelin star.
Spruce is a restaurant in the Presidio Heights neighborhood of San Francisco, California, United States. It serves California / American cuisine.

Wolfsbane is a Michelin-starred restaurant in the Dogpatch neighborhood of San Francisco, California, United States. It opened in 2025 and is co-owned by Rupert and Carrie Blease, the former owners of Lord Stanley, and Tommy Halvorson, the former owner of Serpentine, which was at the location now oc
Naides is a Michelin-starred Filipino restaurant in San Francisco, California, United States.

items.n: Japanese American Museum of San Jose
items.why: The Japanese American Museum of San Jose is located at 535 N. Fifth Street in San Jose, in the heart of Japantown. The museum's mission is to collect, preserve, and share Japanese American art, history, and culture with an emphasis on the Greater San Francisco Bay Area.

The Japanese American National Library is a private non-lending library and resource center in San Francisco's Japantown for the collection and preservation of materials relating to Japanese Americans. It has been in operation since 1969.

John's Grill is a historic restaurant located in the downtown area of San Francisco, California. It is a traditional meeting place for power brokers and politicians, and offers a free lunch on election day.
Kelley Park is a 156-acre (63 ha) city park in San Jose, California, United States.

Kepler's Books and Magazines is an independent bookstore in Menlo Park, California. It was founded on May 14, 1955, by Roy Kepler, a peace activist who had endured multiple internments as a conscientious objector during World War II. Kepler previously had worked as a staff member of radio station KP
Lafayette Park is an 12.5 acres (5.1 ha) park in San Francisco, California, United States.

Lane Medical Library is the library of the Stanford University School of Medicine at Stanford University, near Palo Alto, California. Its mission is to "accelerate scientific discovery, clinical care, medical education and humanities through teaching, collaboration, and delivery of biomedical and hi
Le Papillon is a French restaurant located in San Jose, California.

Leo J. Ryan Memorial Park is a recreational city park, located in Foster City, California and run by the city government and local citizens. Originally called "Central Park", the park was renamed in 1979 in honor and memory of Congressman Leo J. Ryan, who was assassinated in 1978 in Guyana on orders
Recreation Park was the name applied to several former baseball parks in San Francisco, California in the late 19th century and early 20th century.
Rosicrucian Park is the headquarters of the English Grand Lodge for the Americas of the Ancient Mystical Order Rosae Crucis, located in San Jose, California.

Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve is a regional park located in the Santa Cruz Mountains in San Mateo County, California along the San Francisco Peninsula. Its 3,137 acres (1,269 ha) and 10.4 miles (16.7 km) of trails are managed by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District.

SF-88L is a former Nike Missile launch site at Fort Barry, in the Marin Headlands to the north of San Francisco, California, United States. Opened in 1954, the site was intended to protect the population and military installations of the San Francisco Bay Area during the Cold War, specifically from

Sam Wo is a Chinese restaurant located in San Francisco, California. The restaurant's first location on 813 Washington Street was famous for being a venerable mainstay in the local Chinatown area, having been in the same location since 1912.

The Marina Green in San Francisco, California, is a 74-acre (300,000 m2) expanse of grass between Fort Mason and the Presidio. It is adjacent to San Francisco Bay, and this location provides good views of the Golden Gate Bridge, Angel Island, Alcatraz Island, and parts of Marin County.
The Hiller Aviation Museum is an aviation museum located at the San Carlos Airport in San Carlos, California, focused on Northern California aviation history, Hiller Aircraft and helicopter history.

The Musée Mécanique is a for-profit interactive museum of 20th-century penny arcade games and artifacts, located at Fisherman's Wharf in San Francisco, California. With over 300 mechanical machines, it is one of the world's largest privately owned collections.

The de Saisset Museum at Santa Clara University opened in 1955, after Isabel de Saisset, the last member of a California pioneer family bequeathed her estate to the University of Santa Clara. The museum owns nearly 10,000 art pieces and historical artifacts, including the work of early Californian a
The Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum (REM) is a museum devoted to ancient Egypt, located at Rosicrucian Park in the Rose Garden neighborhood of San Jose, California, United States.

The San Jose Municipal Rose Garden is a historic rose garden in San Jose, California, in the Rose Garden District. Founded in 1927, the garden is exclusively dedicated to roses and features more than 3,500 shrubs representing 189 rose varieties.

The Roxie Theater, also known as the Roxie Cinema or just The Roxie, is a historic movie theater, founded in 1912, at 3117 16th Street in the Mission District of San Francisco. It is a non-profit community arthouse cinema.

The Circle Star Theater was a performing arts venue active from 1964 until 1993, located at 2 Circle Star Way in San Carlos, San Mateo County, California, U.S.. Its name is based on it being a theater in the round, featuring a rotating circular stage with none of its 3,743 seats further than 50 feet

South Park is a small urban park and eponymous neighborhood in the larger South of Market neighborhood of San Francisco, California, consisting of 0.85 acres of public ground. The neighborhood centers on the small, oval-shaped park and South Park Street, which encircles the park.

The Marine Mammal Center (TMMC) is a private, non-profit U.S. organization that was established in 1975 for the purpose of rescuing, rehabilitating and releasing marine mammals who are injured, sick or abandoned. It was founded in Sausalito, California, by Lloyd Smalley, Pat Arrigoni and Paul Maxwel

Balboa Park is a public park in the Mission Terrace neighborhood of San Francisco, California. It was originally dedicated in 1909 when the park included the land now used by City College of San Francisco Ocean Campus west of I-280 Freeway.
Stanford Research Park (SRP) is a technology park established in 1951 as a joint initiative between Stanford University and the City of Palo Alto. It was the world's first university research park.
The Cecil H. Green Library is the main library on the Stanford University campus and is part of the SUL system. It is named for Cecil H. Green.

Ainsley House is a 1925 California Arts and Crafts house in Campbell, California, built in the style of an English Tudor Cotswold cottage. The house and accompanying carriage house were listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2005.
The Alcazar Theatre was a 1,145 seat theatre located at 260 O'Farrell Street, San Francisco, California, between Mason and Powell.

The Alcazar Theatre is a 511-seat theatre located at 650 Geary Street, San Francisco, California. The venue is host to many touring productions of Broadway and Off Broadway plays, as well as variety, cabaret, comedians, and other theatrical events. A listed building.

The Alhambra Theatre was a Moorish Revival movie palace at 2330 Polk Street in San Francisco, California, that opened on November 5, 1926. The building was designated a San Francisco landmark in 1996 and currently hosts a Crunch Fitness gym, still showing films on the big screen.

Fremont Older Open Space Preserve is a 739-acre (299 ha) regional park located in Santa Clara County, California and operated by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. The preserve contains 14.7 miles (23.7 km) of hiking trails, nearly all open to equestrians and bicycles.

The Laurence Frost Amphitheater, commonly known as Frost Amphitheater, is a prominent amphitheater at Stanford University. It first opened in 1937 and was the site of commencement ceremonies for the university from 1938 until 1984.

The GLBT Historical Society maintains an extensive collection of archival materials, artifacts and graphic arts relating to LGBTQ history in the United States, with a focus on the LGBTQ communities of San Francisco and Northern California.

Garfield Square, also known as Garfield Park, is a 3.46-acre (14,000 m2) city park located in the Mission District of San Francisco, California. It is bounded by 25th Street to the north, 26th Street to the south, Treat Avenue to the west, and Harrison Street to the east and was first opened in 1884
Glen Canyon Park is a city park in San Francisco, California. It occupies about 70 acres (28 ha) along a deep canyon adjacent to the Glen Park, Diamond Heights, and Miraloma Park neighborhoods.

Grandview Park, also referred to as Turtle Hill by local residents, is a small, elevated park located on the West Side of San Francisco in the city's Sunset District. It is surrounded by 14th and 15th Avenues, as well as Noriega Street.

Gray Whale Cove State Beach is a California State Park between Pacifica, California, and Montara, California, by Highway 1 and approximately 18 miles south of San Francisco. It features a sheltered cove surrounded by abrupt cliffs, with trails connecting to nearby Montara Mountain and McNee Ranch St
Green Apple Books is an independent bookstore in the Richmond District of San Francisco, California.

The Haas–Lilienthal House is a historic building located at 2007 Franklin Street in San Francisco, California, United States, within the Pacific Heights neighborhood. Built in 1886 for William and Bertha Haas, it survived the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and subsequent fire. A listed building.

Half Moon Bay State Beach is a 4-mile (6 km) stretch of protected beaches in the state park system of California, United States, on Half Moon Bay. From north to south it comprises Roosevelt, Dunes, Venice, and Francis Beaches.

The Hall of Transportation, Treasure Island, on Treasure Island, California, also known as Building 2, was built in 1938 for the 1939-40 Golden Gate International Exposition. It served as the hall of transportation for the exposition. A listed building.

Happy Hollow Park & Zoo is a 16-acre (6.5 ha) zoo and amusement park in San Jose, California, which originally opened in 1961. The facility was closed in 2008 for major renovations, and opened its gates again on March 20, 2010.

The Hoover Institution Library and Archives is a research center and archival repository located at Stanford University, near Palo Alto, California in the United States. Built around a collection amassed by Stanford graduate Herbert Hoover prior to his becoming President of the United States, the Ho

The Guadalupe River Park is a city park in San Jose, CA. It is a 120-acre park on the banks of the Guadalupe River for about 2.6 miles in the downtown. It was opened in 2005 after the adjoining section of the river was lined with concrete for flood protection.

The I-Beam was a former popular nightclub and live music venue active from 1977 to 1994, and located in the Park Masonic Hall building on the second floor at 1748 Haight Street in the Haight-Ashbury neighborhood of San Francisco. The I-Beam served as one of San Francisco's earliest disco clubs, as w

The Intel Museum, located at Intel's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, United States, has exhibits of Intel's products and history as well as semiconductor technology in general. The museum is open weekdays except holidays.
